faq.q: Why is the filament made of tungsten?
faq.a: Tungsten has the highest melting point of any metal, about 3400 degrees Celsius, so it can glow white-hot without melting.
asks: What metal is a filament made of?

faq.q: Why doesn't the filament burn up?
faq.a: In air the hot tungsten would burn in a moment. Bulbs hold a vacuum or an unreactive gas like argon, so the filament can last around a thousand hours.
asks: What gas is inside a light bulb?

faq.q: Why are filament bulbs so inefficient?
faq.a: To glow, the filament must be very hot, and a hot object sends out most of its energy as infrared, which we feel as heat but cannot see. Only about 5 percent comes out as visible light.
asks: Why do old bulbs waste energy?

faq.q: Why do old light bulbs get so hot?
faq.a: Around 95 percent of the energy leaves as heat, mostly infrared rays. A 60 watt bulb is like a small heater, so the glass gets far too hot to touch.
asks: Why can't you touch an old bulb?

faq.q: Why do bulbs often blow when you switch them on?
faq.a: A cold filament has low resistance, so a big rush of current flows the moment you switch on. Over time the filament thins in places, and that surge often snaps it.
asks: Why do bulbs pop at switch-on?

facts: Tungsten melts at about 3422 degrees Celsius, the highest melting point of any metal.
LED bulbs use roughly 75 to 85 percent less electricity than filament bulbs for the same light.
